title: Audit the operating file

proposed_identity.status: historical precedent only; L13-L16 purpose-specific rights pending

presenter_passages.passage_exact: At the end of Harbor's Friday, Morgan has a full Operating File. It contains a job, sources, receipts, authority limits, a team handoff, evaluation cases, a proof outline, a research proposal, and a six-beat rehearsal.
Only Morgan and the appropriate owners can make that disposition real. The file gives them a way to see what is ready, what is missing, and what must stop.

offscreen_narration.text:
The file is impressive in one sense: its gaps are visible. Staffing is still unconfirmed. Spend is unapproved. The research test has not run. The board proof has not been shared. The capstone asks whether this design deserves to continue, in what smaller form, and under whose care.

Chapter Twenty-Six names five operating questions: route, log, gate, memory, review. Who receives the work? What record explains it? Where does a human decide? What may be remembered, and by whom? When will someone revisit the rule? The companion workbook expands these into an Accountability Stack from source through rollback. We will use the larger worksheet to audit the single Harbor workflow, while keeping the five questions as a readable spine.

Begin with source and event. Harbor's three course inputs use opaque references and a source-status field. No raw private record belongs in the learner export. The receipt describes a paper event shape; it does not certify that an agent ran. Next, proposal and memory: the staffing rule and source-status rule are proposals until Morgan approves a local plan. A missing approval date stays blank. Do not backfill it to make the stack look complete.

Move to routing, action, approval, and cost. The preparation role may draft a Session Option Brief. Morgan owns the session recommendation. A separate owner must review spend. The agent cannot book, send, buy, or turn a proposal into a team rule. We have no evidence that staffing is available, so the next action is still hold. A capstone score cannot lift that hold. It can identify who must decide and what evidence they need.

Finish with export and rollback. The proof outline is scoped to an audience and remains `not shared`. If a claim is wrong, Harbor can retain the prior draft, correct the paper brief, and record the reason. If a local rule later causes harm, a named owner must be able to narrow, revoke, or retire it. The weakest gate today is staffing confirmation: without it, the brief cannot become a team proposal. That is a useful result, even though nothing launches.

Pause. Pick the weakest gate in your workflow. Would you keep the design as a paper trial, shrink its scope, or retire it? Name the human who can make that call and the evidence that person would need. Use a fictional or approved example. Do not use private operational data. A blank disposition is pending, never consent.

Present your Operating File as a one-page audit. Walk source, event, proposal, memory, routing, action, approval, cost, export, and rollback. For each layer, write owner, evidence, privacy tier, gate, failure mode, and next improvement. Mark missing evidence openly. Then write a human disposition field with decision, owner, date, reason, and next review date. You may leave the decision pending. This is a design review: do not deploy, publish, spend, contact anyone, or run an agent because a worksheet is complete.

Save revision sixteen for review. Morgan's safest current recommendation is to keep the paper design and shrink the next test to staffing evidence and a reviewed brief format.

gates: purpose-specific L13-L16 look and voice approval
fresh provider quote, balance and enforceable one-job and batch caps
native audio timing and sentence-level edit audit
caption, diagram alt, mobile/desktop and final MP4 review
stop_conditions: source, rights, identity, voice or packet drift
uncertain job outcome or provider error; no retry
cost cap uncertainty or unexpected debit
narration omission, repetition or altered meaning
visual clipping, label collision or unreadable captions
